notes: Scope: adults 65 and older in ambulatory, acute and institutional settings; NOT intended for hospice or end-of-life care.

Medications in the criteria are POTENTIALLY inappropriate, not definitely inappropriate. "Avoid" means avoid except under unusual circumstances (e.g., safer alternatives failed); it is not an absolute contraindication unless the label says so. Criteria are not to be used punitively and are meant to support shared decision-making.
Unless stated otherwise, all drugs within a named class are considered potentially inappropriate even if not individually listed (Tables 2-4 footnotes).
Drugs moved off the main tables for low US use or unavailability (Table 8) are still considered PIMs per the 2019 criteria.

Rationale text in this file is paraphrased by MedWatch; it is not a reproduction of the AGS tables. Drug names, classes, thresholds, quality-of-evidence and strength-of-recommendation ratings are recorded as published.

qualityOfEvidence.High: Evidence from one or more well-designed, well-executed RCTs with consistent, directly applicable results; further research very unlikely to change confidence.
qualityOfEvidence.Moderate: RCTs with important limitations, or well-designed non-randomized trials, cohort/case-control studies or time series; further research may change the estimate.
qualityOfEvidence.Low: Typically observational evidence at risk of bias; further research is very likely to change the estimate.
qualityOfEvidence.basis: Synthesis of ACP-based and GRADE-based approaches (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias).

strengthOfRecommendation.Strong: Harms, adverse events and risks clearly outweigh benefits.
strengthOfRecommendation.Weak: Harms, adverse events and risks may not outweigh benefits.

recommendationCodes.avoid: Avoid (AGS meaning: except under unusual circumstances).
recommendationCodes.avoid-conditional: Avoid only in the stated situation (indication, dose, duration, kidney function, sex).
recommendationCodes.avoid-unless: Avoid unless a listed exception applies.
recommendationCodes.avoid-initiation: Avoid starting; existing long-term users may continue or be considered for deprescribing per the entry.
recommendationCodes.avoid-when-possible: Avoid when possible; if used, monitor.
recommendationCodes.Mixed: Rating differs by sub-criterion; see qualityDetail/strengthDetail.

drugs.note: Criterion lists diphenhydramine (oral); topical diphenhydramine products are not covered.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.

conditions.formulation: Diphenhydramine entry is specified as oral.
exceptions: Diphenhydramine may be appropriate for acute treatment of a severe allergic reaction.

pims.rationaleParaphrase: These older allergy, motion-sickness and sleep medicines (common in 'PM' and nighttime products) strongly block acetylcholine, which can cause confusion, dry mouth, constipation and trouble urinating. Repeated use of drugs like this is linked to falls, delirium and dementia, and the sleep effect wears off as the body gets used to it.
pims.clinicianRationale: Highly anticholinergic, with reduced clearance in older adults and tolerance to the hypnotic effect; cumulative anticholinergic exposure is associated with falls, delirium and dementia, so total anticholinergic burden should be reviewed in both young-old and old-old adults. Acute diphenhydramine for severe allergic reactions may be appropriate.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: rationale expanded to address cumulative anticholinergic burden. Carbinoxamine, clemastine, dexchlorpheniramine (low use) and dexbrompheniramine, pyrilamine (not on US market) were moved off the main tables but remain PIMs per 2019 (Table 8).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid in people with CrCl <30 mL/min or for long-term suppression.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: This bladder-infection antibiotic can harm the lungs, liver and nerves, especially when taken for a long time. It should be avoided for long-term prevention and when kidney function is low, because safer choices exist.
pims.clinicianRationale: Risk of lung toxicity, liver toxicity and peripheral neuropathy, greatest with prolonged courses; safer options exist. Not for patients whose CrCl is below 30 mL/min or for long-term UTI prophylaxis (also listed in Table 6).
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged in Table 2; duplicated into Table 6 in 2023 for usability.

pims.drugClass: Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease

drugs.note: Applies only when the indication is primary prevention (no established cardiovascular disease).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid starting aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease; consider deprescribing in older adults already taking it for primary prevention.

conditions.indication: Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease only
notApplicable: Secondary prevention in established cardiovascular disease (aspirin is generally indicated)

pims.rationaleParaphrase: For older adults who have never had a heart attack or stroke, the bleeding risk from daily aspirin rises sharply with age and studies show no overall benefit from starting it. People with established heart or blood-vessel disease usually should stay on aspirin, so changes should only be made with the prescriber.
pims.clinicianRationale: Major bleeding risk climbs steeply with age, and trial data show no net benefit (and possible net harm) from starting aspirin for primary prevention in older adults; data on stopping in long-term users are sparser, though the same logic may apply. Aspirin generally remains indicated for secondary prevention in established CVD.
pims.changeVs2019: Moved from Table 4 (2019: 'use with caution' in adults >=70) to Table 2 (avoid initiating; consider deprescribing), consistent with the 2022 USPSTF recommendation.

pims.drugClass: Warfarin for treatment of nonvalvular atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism
pims.recommendationText: Avoid starting warfarin as initial therapy for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation or VTE unless DOACs are contraindicated or there are substantial barriers to their use. For long-term warfarin users, continuing may be reasonable, particularly with well-controlled INR (>70% time in therapeutic range) and no adverse effects.

exceptions: Substantial barriers to DOAC use (e.g., cost, access)
Long-term users with well-controlled INR (time in therapeutic range >70%) and no adverse effects may reasonably continue

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Compared with newer blood thinners (DOACs such as apixaban), warfarin causes more serious bleeding, especially in the brain, and works no better for atrial fibrillation or blood clots. People who have been stable on warfarin for a long time may reasonably stay on it, so this is a topic to discuss, not a reason to stop.
pims.clinicianRationale: Versus DOACs, warfarin carries higher major bleeding risk (particularly intracranial) with similar or lower effectiveness for NVAF and VTE, so DOACs are preferred for most patients. Continuation may be reasonable in long-term users with well-controlled INR (TTR >70%) and no adverse effects.
pims.changeVs2019: New criterion in 2023.

pims.drugClass: Rivaroxaban for long-term treatment of nonvalvular atrial fibrillation or VTE
pims.recommendationText: Avoid for long-term treatment of atrial fibrillation or VTE in favor of safer anticoagulant alternatives.

indication: Long-term treatment of nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
exceptions: May be reasonable in special situations, e.g., when once-daily dosing is necessary to support adherence

pims.rationaleParaphrase: When used long term for atrial fibrillation or blood clots, rivaroxaban appears to cause more major and stomach or intestinal bleeding in older adults than other similar blood thinners, particularly apixaban. It can still be reasonable in some cases (for example when once-a-day dosing really helps), so alternatives should be discussed with the prescriber rather than stopping it.
pims.clinicianRationale: At doses used for long-term NVAF or VTE treatment, rivaroxaban appears to confer higher major and GI bleeding risk in older adults than other DOACs, especially apixaban; all DOACs have lower intracranial hemorrhage risk than warfarin. May be reasonable when once-daily dosing is needed for adherence.
pims.changeVs2019: Moved from Table 4 (2019: 'use with caution' for VTE or AF treatment in adults >=75) to Table 2 'avoid'.

drugs.note: Oral short-acting only; does not apply to the extended-release dipyridamole/aspirin combination or IV use for cardiac stress testing.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.

notApplicable: IV dipyridamole for cardiac stress testing (acceptable)

pims.rationaleParaphrase: This older blood-flow medicine can make blood pressure drop when standing up, raising the chance of dizziness and falls. More effective alternatives exist.
pims.clinicianRationale: May cause orthostatic hypotension; more effective alternatives are available. IV form is acceptable for cardiac stress testing.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.drugClass: Non-selective peripheral alpha-1 blockers for treatment of hypertension
pims.recommendationText: Avoid use as an antihypertensive.

notApplicable: Use for other indications (e.g., urinary symptoms of BPH) is not addressed by this Table 2 criterion; see Table 3 (syncope; urinary incontinence in women) and Table 5 (with loop diuretics).

pims.rationaleParaphrase: When used to treat high blood pressure, these medicines often cause blood pressure to drop on standing, which can lead to dizziness, fainting and falls. Other blood pressure medicines usually work better with fewer risks.
pims.clinicianRationale: Orthostatic hypotension and its downstream harms are common in older adults; other antihypertensive classes offer a better risk/benefit balance, so these agents are not routine hypertension therapy.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged (individual drugs now listed).

pims.drugClass: Central alpha-agonists for treatment of hypertension
pims.recommendationText: Avoid clonidine as first-line treatment for hypertension. Avoid other central alpha-agonists for the treatment of hypertension.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: These blood pressure medicines often affect the brain (sleepiness, confusion) and can slow the heart or cause dizziness on standing. They are not recommended as routine blood pressure treatment.
pims.clinicianRationale: Frequent CNS adverse effects plus bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension; not appropriate as routine antihypertensive therapy.
pims.changeVs2019: Guanabenz, methyldopa and reserpine (>0.1 mg/day) moved off main tables because they are not on the US market (Table 8).

drugs.note: Immediate-release formulation only (in the US, generic capsules). Extended-release nifedipine is not covered; current RxNorm Procardia (XL), Adalat CC and Afeditab CR products are all extended-release, so these brand names must NOT trigger this criterion.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: The short-acting form of nifedipine can drop blood pressure suddenly and may reduce blood flow to the heart. Long-acting forms are not part of this warning.
pims.clinicianRationale: Potential for hypotension and risk of precipitating myocardial ischemia.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid as first-line therapy for atrial fibrillation unless the patient has heart failure or substantial left ventricular hypertrophy.

exceptions: Substantial left ventricular hypertrophy (when rhythm control is preferred over rate control)

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Amiodarone is good at keeping a normal heart rhythm but has more serious side effects than other rhythm medicines used for atrial fibrillation. It can still be a reasonable first choice for people who also have heart failure or a substantially thickened heart muscle.
pims.clinicianRationale: Maintains sinus rhythm effectively but is more toxic than other AF antiarrhythmics; may be a reasonable first-line rhythm-control choice when heart failure or substantial LVH coexists.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid in permanent atrial fibrillation or severe or recently decompensated heart failure. Use caution in HFrEF with less severe symptoms (NYHA class I or II).

avoidIn: Severe or recently decompensated heart failure
cautionIn: HFrEF with NYHA class I-II symptoms (e.g., LVEF <=35%)

pims.rationaleParaphrase: This heart-rhythm medicine has been linked to worse outcomes in people whose atrial fibrillation is permanent or whose heart failure is severe or recently worsened. Extra caution is needed even in milder heart failure with a weak heart pump.
pims.clinicianRationale: Worse outcomes in permanent AF and in severe or recently decompensated HF; worse outcomes have also been reported in some circumstances in HFrEF (e.g., LVEF <=35%) with NYHA class I-II symptoms.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: added caution for HFrEF with less severe (NYHA I-II) symptoms.

pims.drugClass: Digoxin for first-line treatment of atrial fibrillation or heart failure
pims.recommendationText: Avoid as first-line rate-control therapy for atrial fibrillation. Avoid as first-line therapy for heart failure (use caution withdrawing it in long-term users with HFrEF). If used for atrial fibrillation or heart failure, avoid dosages >0.125 mg/day.

conditions.renal: Further dose reduction may be needed in CKD stage 4 or 5.
cautions: Use caution discontinuing in current users with HFrEF (limited evidence of worse outcomes after withdrawal).

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Safer and more effective medicines are usually tried first for atrial fibrillation and heart failure, and digoxin doses above 0.125 mg a day add toxicity risk without extra benefit. Stopping digoxin in someone with a weak heart pump who has taken it for a long time also needs care, so any change should be made by the prescriber.
pims.clinicianRationale: Not first-line for AF rate control (safer, more effective alternatives) or HF (stronger evidence for other agents in HFrEF); higher doses add no benefit and may increase toxicity, and reduced renal clearance raises toxicity risk. Limited evidence suggests worse outcomes after discontinuation in HFrEF.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: added caution about discontinuing digoxin in current users with HFrEF.

pims.drugClass: Antidepressants with strong anticholinergic activity, alone or in combination

drugs.note: Only doses >6 mg/day; low-dose doxepin (<=6 mg/day, e.g., for sleep) is excluded.

brandsLikelyOutOfScope.Silenor: Doxepin 3-6 mg tablets; <=6 mg/day is excluded

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: These antidepressants (older 'tricyclics' and paroxetine) strongly block acetylcholine, cause drowsiness, and can make blood pressure drop on standing. Very low-dose doxepin for sleep (6 mg a day or less) is not included.
pims.clinicianRationale: Highly anticholinergic, sedating, and cause orthostatic hypotension; low-dose doxepin (<=6 mg/day) has a safety profile comparable to placebo.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: clarified that the criterion refers to antidepressants with strong anticholinergic activity. Protriptyline and trimipramine moved off main tables (low use; Table 8).

pims.drugClass: Antiparkinsonian agents with strong anticholinergic activity
pims.recommendationText: Avoid.

conditions.formulation: Benztropine entry is specified as oral.

pims.rationaleParaphrase: These medicines are not recommended for preventing or treating movement side effects from antipsychotic drugs, and better options exist for Parkinson disease. They are also strongly anticholinergic.
pims.clinicianRationale: Not recommended for prevention or treatment of antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal symptoms; more effective agents are available for Parkinson disease.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid, except in FDA-approved indications such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, Parkinson disease psychosis, adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder, or short-term use as an antiemetic.

exceptions: Adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder
conditions.dementiaOrDelirium: Avoid for behavioral problems of dementia or delirium unless documented nonpharmacologic options have failed and/or the patient is threatening substantial harm to self or others; if used, periodically attempt deprescribing to reassess need and lowest effective dose.

pims.rationaleParaphrase: In people with dementia, antipsychotic medicines raise the risk of stroke, faster memory decline and death, and they are linked to higher death rates even without dementia. They are generally reserved for specific psychiatric conditions, with non-drug approaches tried first for agitation or behavior changes.
pims.clinicianRationale: Increased risk of stroke, faster cognitive decline and mortality in dementia, plus evidence of increased mortality independent of dementia. For behavioral symptoms of dementia or delirium, use only after documented failure of nonpharmacologic approaches and/or substantial threat of harm, with periodic deprescribing attempts.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: updated language reflecting new evidence (mortality independent of dementia; deprescribing attempts); thioridazine, loxapine, trifluoperazine removed for low use (Table 8).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: Barbiturates (including butalbital in some headache pills) easily cause physical dependence, stop helping sleep over time, and can lead to overdose even at low doses.
pims.clinicianRationale: Physical dependence is common, hypnotic benefit fades with tolerance, and overdose can occur at relatively low doses.
pims.changeVs2019: Amobarbital, butobarbital, mephobarbital, pentobarbital and secobarbital moved off main tables (low use or not on US market; Table 8).

drugs.note: Alone or combined with amitriptyline or clidinium.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.

exceptions: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Benzodiazepines (for anxiety or sleep) make older adults more prone to memory problems, confusion, falls, broken bones and car crashes, and can cause dependence; combined with opioid pain medicines they can dangerously slow breathing. They should not be stopped suddenly after regular use, so any reduction should be a gradual plan made with the prescriber.
pims.clinicianRationale: Carry risks of abuse, misuse, addiction and clinically significant physical dependence; older adults are more sensitive, clear long-acting agents slowly, and show higher rates of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures and car crashes with any benzodiazepine. Co-prescription with opioids can produce profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death.

safetyNote.text: Taper advice: FDA Drug Safety Communication (2020) requiring updated boxed warning for benzodiazepines (abrupt discontinuation can cause serious withdrawal reactions).

pims.changeVs2019: Modified: clarified language, added abuse/misuse/addiction and opioid co-use risks; flurazepam and quazepam removed for low use (Table 8).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: These sleeping pills carry risks similar to benzodiazepines in older adults, including confusion, falls, fractures, emergency visits and car crashes, while improving sleep only slightly.
pims.clinicianRationale: Adverse events similar to benzodiazepines (delirium, falls, fractures, ED visits/hospitalizations, motor vehicle crashes) with minimal improvement in sleep latency and duration.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: This older anti-anxiety medicine is very sedating and easily causes physical dependence.
pims.clinicianRationale: High rate of physical dependence; very sedating.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: This medicine has not been shown to work.
pims.clinicianRationale: Lack of efficacy.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged (isoxsuprine removed: not on US market).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid unless indicated for confirmed hypogonadism with clinical symptoms.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: Testosterone products may cause heart problems and carry potential risks for men with prostate cancer. They are mainly appropriate for men with confirmed low testosterone that is causing symptoms.
pims.clinicianRationale: Possible cardiac harms, and potential (no longer described as contraindicated) risk for men with prostate cancer.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: prostate cancer language changed from 'contraindicated' to 'potential risks'.

pims.drugClass: Estrogens with or without progestins (natural and synthetic preparations)

drugs.note: Class member; systemic (oral/transdermal) products are covered; low-dose vaginal products are acceptable.
Class member; vaginal cream use is acceptable at low dose.

pims.recommendationText: Do not initiate systemic estrogen (e.g., oral tablets or transdermal patches); consider deprescribing among older women already using it. Low-dose intravaginal estrogen (cream or tablets) is acceptable for dyspareunia, recurrent lower urinary tract infections and other vaginal symptoms.

conditions.formulation: Systemic (oral, transdermal) = avoid initiating; vaginal cream/tablets at low dose = acceptable
conditions.breastCancerHistory: Women with prior breast cancer not responding to nonhormonal therapy should discuss low-dose vaginal estrogen (e.g., estradiol <25 mcg twice weekly) with their clinician.
conditions.ageNote: For women starting HRT at age 60 or older, risks exceed benefits.

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Estrogen pills and patches raise the risk of breast and uterine cancer and do not protect the heart or memory, and starting hormone therapy at 60 or older brings more risk (heart disease, stroke, blood clots, dementia) than benefit. Low-dose vaginal estrogen for dryness or repeated bladder infections is considered safe and effective.
pims.clinicianRationale: Carcinogenic potential (breast, endometrium) and no cardioprotective or cognitive benefit; for women starting HRT at >=60, risks (heart disease, stroke, VTE, dementia) exceed benefits. Vaginal estrogen for vaginal dryness is safe and effective.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: 'do not initiate' systemic estrogen and consider deprescribing; added data on risks when HRT is started at age >=60.

pims.drugClass: Insulin, sliding scale (short- or rapid-acting insulin only, dosed to current glucose, without basal/long-acting insulin)

drugs.note: Only when used as the sole insulin in a glucose-based sliding scale.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid insulin regimens containing only short- or rapid-acting insulin dosed according to current blood glucose without concurrent basal or long-acting insulin.

conditions.regimen: Short/rapid-acting insulin only, dosed by current glucose
notApplicable: Regimens that include basal or long-acting insulin

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Using only fast-acting insulin adjusted to each blood sugar reading, without a long-acting 'background' insulin, causes more low blood sugar episodes without improving overall control. This does not apply when a long-acting insulin is part of the plan.
pims.clinicianRationale: Raises hypoglycemia risk without better glycemic control in any care setting; regimens that include basal or long-acting insulin are not covered.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

drugs.note: Not marketed in the US; listed by AGS.
Short-acting (preferred if a sulfonylurea must be used).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid sulfonylureas as first- or second-line monotherapy or add-on therapy unless there are substantial barriers to the use of safer and more effective agents. If a sulfonylurea is used, choose short-acting agents (e.g., glipizide) over long-acting agents (e.g., glyburide, glimepiride).

exceptions: Substantial barriers (e.g., cost) to safer, more effective agents

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Compared with other diabetes medicines, sulfonylureas cause more low blood sugar episodes and are linked to more heart problems and deaths. If one is needed, shorter-acting glipizide carries less risk of long-lasting low blood sugar than glyburide or glimepiride.
pims.clinicianRationale: Compared with alternative agents, sulfonylureas are associated with more cardiovascular events, higher all-cause mortality and more hypoglycemia, with possible increases in CV death and ischemic stroke; long-acting agents (glyburide, glimepiride) cause more prolonged hypoglycemia than short-acting glipizide.
pims.changeVs2019: Expanded from long-acting sulfonylureas only (2019: chlorpropamide, glimepiride, glyburide; High/Strong) to all sulfonylureas; chlorpropamide removed (not on US market).

drugs.note: RxNorm ingredient name for desiccated (animal) thyroid.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: Animal-derived thyroid tablets raise concerns about effects on the heart, and safer thyroid replacement is available.
pims.clinicianRationale: Concerns about cardiac effects; safer alternatives available.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: Often used to boost appetite, megestrol adds little weight but raises the risk of blood clots and possibly death in older adults.
pims.clinicianRationale: Little weight-gain benefit; raises thrombosis risk and possibly mortality in older adults.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid, except for patients rigorously diagnosed by evidence-based criteria with growth hormone deficiency due to an established etiology.

exceptions: Rigorously diagnosed growth hormone deficiency with an established cause

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Growth hormone changes body composition only slightly and is linked to swelling, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, breast enlargement and higher fasting blood sugar.
pims.clinicianRationale: Body-composition benefit is small, while gynecomastia, edema, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthralgia and impaired fasting glucose occur.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid scheduled use for >8 weeks unless for high-risk patients (e.g., oral corticosteroids or chronic NSAID use), erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagitis, pathologic hypersecretory condition, or demonstrated need for maintenance treatment (e.g., failed drug discontinuation trial or failed H2-receptor antagonists).

exceptions: High-risk patients (e.g., oral corticosteroids or chronic NSAID use)
Demonstrated need for maintenance (failed discontinuation trial or failed H2-receptor antagonist)

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Taking a PPI acid reducer every day for more than 8 weeks is linked to a serious gut infection (C. difficile), pneumonia, bone loss and fractures, and stomach or intestinal cancers. Many people do need long-term PPIs for specific conditions, so ask whether daily use is still needed rather than stopping on your own.
pims.clinicianRationale: Linked to C. difficile infection, bone loss and fractures, pneumonia, and GI cancers; scheduled use beyond 8 weeks should be confined to high-risk patients or the listed indications.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: pneumonia and GI malignancies added to rationale (2019 rationale: C. difficile, bone loss, fractures).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid, unless for gastroparesis with a duration of use not to exceed 12 weeks except in rare cases.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: Metoclopramide can cause movement problems, including involuntary movements called tardive dyskinesia, and the risk is higher in frail older adults and with longer use.
pims.clinicianRationale: Extrapyramidal effects including tardive dyskinesia, with higher risk among frail older adults and with longer exposure.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.drugClass: GI antispasmodics with strong anticholinergic activity

drugs.note: Listed as clidinium-chlordiazepoxide (e.g., Librax); the chlordiazepoxide component is also covered by the benzodiazepine criterion.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: These stomach-cramp medicines are strongly anticholinergic and it is unclear how well they work.
pims.clinicianRationale: Highly anticholinergic, uncertain effectiveness.
pims.changeVs2019: Belladonna alkaloids, propantheline (not on US market) and methscopolamine (low use) moved off main tables (Table 8).

drugs.note: Oral use only (topical, ophthalmic and rectal products are not covered).

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: Swallowed mineral oil (a laxative) can accidentally be breathed into the lungs and has other side effects; safer laxatives are available.
pims.clinicianRationale: Aspiration risk and other adverse effects; safer laxatives exist.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid for treatment of nocturia or nocturnal polyuria.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: When used for waking at night to urinate, desmopressin carries a high risk of dangerously low blood sodium; safer options, including non-drug approaches, exist.
pims.clinicianRationale: Hyponatremia risk is high; safer nocturia management, including nondrug measures, is available.
pims.changeVs2019: Unchanged.

drugs.note: Only at doses >325 mg/day under this criterion.
Oral only. Topical diclofenac (e.g., Voltaren Arthritis Pain gel, Flector, Pennsaid) is not covered; current RxNorm 'Voltaren' products are topical gel.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid chronic use unless other alternatives are not effective and the patient can take a gastroprotective agent (PPI or misoprostol). Avoid short-term scheduled use together with oral or parenteral corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents unless other alternatives are not effective and the patient can take a gastroprotective agent.

conditions.duration: Chronic use; or short-term scheduled use when combined with corticosteroids, anticoagulants or antiplatelets
conditions.mitigation: PPI or misoprostol reduces but does not eliminate risk

pims.rationaleParaphrase: Regular use of anti-inflammatory pain relievers such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) and naproxen (Aleve) raises the risk of stomach bleeding and ulcers, especially after age 75 or with steroids or blood thinners, and can also raise blood pressure and harm the kidneys. The risk grows with dose and length of use, and a stomach-protecting medicine lowers it but does not remove it.
pims.clinicianRationale: Increased GI bleeding/peptic ulcer risk in high-risk groups (age >75; corticosteroids, anticoagulants or antiplatelets); upper GI ulcers, bleeding or perforation occur in roughly 1% of patients treated 3-6 months and 2-4% treated 1 year. Also can raise blood pressure and cause kidney injury; risks are dose-related.
pims.changeVs2019: Modified: added avoidance of short-term scheduled use with corticosteroids, anticoagulants or antiplatelets (absorbs the former Table 5 warfarin+NSAID and corticosteroid+NSAID interactions); fenoprofen, ketoprofen, meclofenamate, mefenamic acid (low use) and tolmetin (not on US market) moved off main tables.

pims.recommendationText: Avoid.
pims.rationaleParaphrase: These two anti-inflammatory drugs carry especially high risks of stomach bleeding, ulcers and sudden kidney injury in older adults, and indomethacin has more side effects on the brain and nervous system than other NSAIDs.

useWithCaution.recommendationText: Use caution in selecting dabigatran over other DOACs (e.g., apixaban) for long-term treatment of nonvalvular AF or VTE.

useWithCaution.clinicianRationale: Higher GI bleeding vs warfarin (head-to-head trials) and higher GI and major bleeding vs apixaban (observational studies, meta-analyses) when used long term for NVAF or VTE in older adults. anticoagulantSummary.summary: Box 1 synthesizes the anticoagulant criteria: warfarin (Table 2: avoid starting as initial therapy for VTE or nonvalvular AF unless DOACs are contraindicated or there are substantial barriers; long-term users with well-controlled INR may reasonably continue), rivaroxaban (Table 2: avoid for long-term NVAF/VTE treatment in favor of safer alternatives) and dabigatran (Table 4: use caution in selecting it over other DOACs such as apixaban). implementationNotes: MedWatch-specific guidance (not AGS text): present every match as a question for the clinician/pharmacist, never as an instruction to stop or change a medicine.

Many criteria need context beyond the drug name (indication, dose, duration, formulation/route, kidney function, sex, diagnoses). When context is missing, show the criterion with "needs clinician confirmation" rather than asserting inappropriateness.

Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, antidepressants, antiepileptics, opioids and other CNS-active drugs should not be stopped abruptly; FDA requires boxed-warning language that abrupt benzodiazepine discontinuation can cause serious withdrawal reactions (https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-requiring-boxed-warning-updated-improve-safe-use-benzodiazepine-drug-class).

combinationMembers lists (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, dextromethorphan-quinidine) match only when ALL listed ingredients are present in the same product or regimen; the single ingredients alone do not match those criteria.
Combination products: resolve brand names to all ingredients (brandIndex) before applying class rules (e.g., Tylenol PM -> acetaminophen + diphenhydramine; Advil PM -> ibuprofen + diphenhydramine).
Count distinct drugs (not classes) for the >=2 anticholinergic and >=3 CNS-active rules; a drug belonging to two classes counts once.
Topical, ophthalmic and otic products are generally outside the oral/systemic criteria (e.g., Table 2 NSAIDs are oral; atropine excludes ophthalmic).
